rule: Constructor / initializer call: `Type#<init>`. ... Free function: its name (with the language's module qualifier ...) ... Kotlin top-level functions `com.x.f`. ... Companion-object members flatten onto the class. ... Overloads share one ID.
source: KNOWN_GAP: companion operator invoke and factory functions named like a type are reported as constructors
notes: call_type convention (SPEC names the six call_types but does not define direct vs method): a call with no written receiver is direct; a call with a written receiver (obj., this., super., a type or object name) is method; a class-name call `T(..)` that resolves to a constructor, and `: this(..)` / `: super(..)` / a supertype-list call, are constructor. Kotlin has no `new`; a `val x = T(..)` constructor call is treated as decision A's `= new T(...)`. Kotlin resolves `Parser(3)` (Int) to the companion's `operator fun invoke(n: Int)`, because the only constructor takes a String. It runs `Parser.Companion.invoke(3)`, so the callee is the flattened companion member Parser#invoke, not Parser#<init>. call_type is method because the companion object `Parser` is the receiver of the desugared `Parser.invoke(3)`. `Parser("q")` matches the constructor: Parser#<init>. `fun Token(text: String)` is a top-level function, ID `com.acme.parse.Token`. `Token("a")` (one argument) resolves to it: direct, high, not Token#<init>. `Token("b", 1)` matches the class constructor. Inside the factory, `Token(text, 0)` is the constructor, caller `com.acme.parse.Token`.
